newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Fate of Romania Petromidia refinery still unclear.
newsitem.headline: Fate of Romania Petromidia refinery still unclear.

text.p: Romania's government will decide this week the fate of the Petromidia SA oil refinery which the reformist cabinet included among loss-making firms shortlisted for closure, the reform minister said on Tuesday.
"We will find a solution for Petromidia within the next days," Ulm Spineanu told a news conference.

Last week, the government said it planned to close Petromidia and nine other loss-making companies as part of moves to restructure oversized industries in line with suggestions made by international lenders.
The move was bitterly attacked by Petromidia's management and by trade unions.
Petromidia's losses amounted to some 300 billion lei in 1996, or 4.9 percent of total losses recorded by Romania's economy last year.
Its managers blamed the losses on what they called an inappropriate pricing and a lack of funds to import crued to keep the plant running efficiently.
"We will analyse Petromidia's situation. The problem is that there are huge discrepancies between their (Petromidia's) data and our figures," Spineanu said.
A government statement said on Tuesday Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea had suggested a partial cut in the refinery's activity in order to recoup losses.

Under the plan, Petromidia would honour current contracts but no other funds would be made available for investments, the statement said. The government, it said, "will select the most suitable foreign investor for Petromidia's privatisation."
Refinery officials were unavailable for comment.

Petromidia was built in the 1980s, with good access to export markets via the Black Sea. It operates a single train of 70,000 barrels a day and can produce a full range of main fuel products and coking coal. It also has a petrochemical plant.

It underwent a $50 million modernisation in 1993 to improve its performance. But analysts said the performance was achieved only by increasing Petrmidia's indebtness to such an extent that the refinery found it difficult to meet its obligations.
Romania has a processing capacity of 34 million tonnes a year, exceeding by far the country's needs.
Ciorbea has vowed tough action to cut losses in industry. Romania is seeking some $400 million in International Monetary Fund credits and $600 million from the World Bank.
